source: Steegen, Dewitte, Tuerlinckx, Vanpaemel (2014) Measuring the crowd within again: a pre-registered replication
finding: A large pre-registered replication of Vul and Pashler (2008) confirmed that averaging two guesses from one person beats a single guess, both right away and after a 3-week delay.
numbers: Immediate: N=471 analysed. MSE of average 541 vs guess 1 589 (t(470)=8.69, dz=0.40, CI 0.31-0.49) and guess 2 615 (dz=0.47). Delayed 3 weeks: N=140. MSE of average 467 vs guess 1 517 (dz=0.34) and guess 2 589 (dz=0.72). Second guesses were worse than first (dz=-0.10 immediate).
quote: We successfully replicated the crowd within effect, both when the second guess was made immediately after the first guess
limits: Psychology students at one university, 8 general-knowledge questions. Earlier immediate replications were mixed: Herzog and Hertwig 2009 had a CI that included zero; an unpublished replication failed (reported by Vul). Effect is small (dz 0.3-0.5).
agent_relevance: Resampling the same model gives a small gain, not a crowd. Independence is bought by delay and difference. Same-model samples at one prompt are the immediate, low-independence case (supports G4).

source: Steegen et al. (2014) review section on prior crowd-within replications
finding: Of four earlier tries to replicate the immediate crowd-within effect, two succeeded (Hourihan and Benjamin 2010; Rauhut and Lorenz 2011), one had a confidence interval including zero (Herzog and Hertwig 2009), and one unpublished attempt failed.
numbers: 4 attempts: 2 clear successes, 1 borderline, 1 failure. Delayed condition had no prior replication before 2014.
limits: Counts are as reported by Steegen et al., not re-checked against the originals.
agent_relevance: Expect an inconsistent gain from cheap re-asking; do not build a design on a gain that fails in a quarter to half of attempts.

source: Lorenz, Rauhut, Schweitzer, Helbing (2011) How social influence can undermine the wisdom of crowd effect, PNAS 108(22)
finding: Showing people each other's estimates shrank the spread of answers without making the group mean more accurate, pushed the truth toward the edge of the guess range, and raised confidence.
numbers: 144 ETH students, 12 sessions of 12, 6 factual questions, 5 rounds; 3 conditions (no info, mean shown, all estimates shown), 24 groups per condition. Arithmetic mean beat individuals' first guesses in only 21.3% of cases; on log scale 77.1%. Median error vs truth e.g. border length -59.1%, assaults -56.9%.
quote: even mild social influence can undermine the wisdom of crowd effect in simple estimation tasks
limits: Small student sample, hard numeric questions with skewed answers, truth often in the tail. p-values only in the SI. Later work (Becker 2017, Almaatouq 2021) shows the harm depends on network and answer distribution.
agent_relevance: Letting agents see each other's answers before voting cuts diversity for no gain. Collect answers blind, then compare (G4, G5).

source: Becker, Brackbill, Centola (2017) Network dynamics of social influence in the wisdom of crowds, PNAS
finding: In decentralised networks social influence made the group mean more accurate; in centralised networks it helped or hurt depending on whether the central person started near the truth.
numbers: 1,360 people; 40 per network; 520 per network condition, 320 control. Decentralised: mean error 0.69 to 0.62 (-10%), median -12%, individual error -23%, SD -43%. Control: no significant change. Centralised, central node toward truth: mean error -43%; away from truth: +19% (median +32%).
quote: Remarkably, however, we found that, on average, each group's mean estimate also became more accurate.
limits: 13 trials per network condition (each network is one observation). 40-person networks, paid web tasks, count and percentage questions.
agent_relevance: Contradicts Lorenz 2011: influence is not always harmful. The risk is a single hub whose answer spreads. Any scaffold that lets one agent's draft steer others is a centralised network (G5: no majority or proposed answer shown to the judge).

source: Almaatouq, Rahimian, Burton, Alhajri (2021) When social influence promotes the wisdom of crowds
finding: Reconciles the conflicting results: whether influence helps depends on how centralised the influence network is and on the shape of the starting estimates. Skewed, heavy-tailed starts favour centralised weighting; centred starts favour decentralised.
numbers: Theory plus simulation plus reanalysis of 4 published datasets, 2,885 human subjects in total.
quote: the wisdom of crowds critically depends on the interaction between (i) the centralization of the social influence network and (ii) the distribution of the initial, individual estimates
limits: Positive numeric estimation tasks only. Assumes weights are a fixed averaging rule.
agent_relevance: The mean of heavy-tailed errors is dominated by a few egregious answers. For numeric answers use median or trimmed mean in code, not mean (G5).

source: Kao, Berdahl, Couzin (2018) Counteracting estimation bias and social influence to improve the wisdom of crowds, J R Soc Interface
finding: Standard aggregates (mean, median, geometric mean) are biased on jar-counting tasks and degrade under social influence; distribution-based corrected estimators are robust to influence.
numbers: 812 people over 5 new jar datasets (sizes 54 to 27,852); 602 in the 659-object Princeton social influence experiment (231 ignored social info, 371 used it). New estimators beat standard ones in 58-78% of simulations. Needed training samples: max-likelihood >=20, corrected mean >=105, corrected median >=175. Hidden-expert weighting showed no benefit (p=0.938).
limits: Jar-counting only; simulated influence on a fully connected network only; needs training data from similar tasks.
agent_relevance: Bias that is shared by all voters cannot be voted away. A calibration on past tasks can fix it; a bigger sample cannot.

source: Frey and van de Rijt (2021) Social influence undermines the wisdom of the crowd in sequential decision making, Management Science 67(7)
finding: When people choose in sequence and see earlier tallies, individual votes get more accurate but majorities get worse; early errors cascade, and on hard questions wrong majorities do not self-correct.
numbers: Lab: groups of 10-14, 30 A-or-B questions. Online follow-up: 100 subjects on the same question.
limits: Read through search summaries only, not the paper text. Binary questions.
agent_relevance: Sequential debate or critique where later agents see earlier answers is the cascade setting. Parallel blind samples avoid it (G4).

source: Prelec, Seung, McCoy (2017) A solution to the single-question crowd wisdom problem, Nature 541
finding: Plain majority vote fails when the crowd shares a wrong belief. Choose the answer that is more popular than people predicted (surprisingly popular), which reduces errors in several studies.
numbers: Simulations in the text: a 90% majority is right about 90% of the time; a 55% majority is not much better than chance. Studies 1-4 included state capitals and 20th-century artwork prices (details in figures not read).
quote: A majority of 90% is correct about 90% of the time, while a majority of 55% is not much better than chance.
limits: Page text was only partly available (abstract, intro, parts of methods). Needs each respondent to also predict others' answers. Assumes some respondents hold information others lack.
agent_relevance: A narrow majority from one model family is weak evidence. Asking samples to predict what other samples will say is a code-level check we can test, but G4 warns against extremizing votes.

source: Karge (2025) When Diversity in Voting Trumps Ability, Episteme
finding: The Hong-Page Diversity-Trumps-Ability theorem has been criticised for weak mathematics (Thompson 2014). This paper sets exact conditions under which a more diverse group beats a more able one in a Condorcet-style voting model with an opinion leader.
numbers: Theory paper; no empirical numbers.
quote: Despite considerable criticism regarding the DTA's mathematical rigor, it has sparked substantial interdisciplinary discussion.
limits: Formal model with one kind of dependence (an opinion leader). Thompson 2014 itself was not opened (403).
agent_relevance: Diversity beats ability only under conditions. Do not assume a weaker, different voter always helps. Test it.

source: Hong and Page (2004) Groups of diverse problem solvers can outperform groups of high-ability problem solvers, PNAS
finding: Computer experiment and theorem: a random group of agents with different heuristics can beat a group of the individually best agents at a search task.
numbers: Not re-read this session. Recalled setup: 20 agents drawn from 2000 heuristics, best 10 versus random 10; check before using.
limits: Thompson (2014, AMS Notices) argues the theorem needs strong assumptions and the headline is over-read. The source page was not fetched; from memory only.
agent_relevance: The famous claim behind persona and strategy voters. G4 already bans persona voters on single-answer problems; this is the main evidence people cite against that.

source: Galton (1907) Vox Populi, Nature 75
finding: The median of about 800 fair-goers' guesses at an ox's dressed weight was within about 1% of the true weight.
numbers: From memory and secondary accounts: 787 usable tickets; true weight 1198 lb; median 1207 lb. File fetched but is a scan with no text layer, so not verified here.
limits: One animal, one fair, not independent samples. Galton chose the median and noted it from the middle of a skewed spread.
agent_relevance: The founding case uses a median of a numeric answer, not a majority over labels.

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd
finding: The median of 12 different LLMs forecasting 31 binary questions was statistically indistinguishable from a 925-person human crowd, and better than guessing 50%.
numbers: LLM crowd Brier 0.20 (SD 0.12) vs human crowd 0.19 (SD 0.19), t(60)=0.19, p=0.850; no-information benchmark 0.25. Best single model GPT-4 0.15; Claude 2 0.21; GPT-3.5-Instruct and Llama-2-70B 0.25; Coral 0.38. Models were biased high (acquiescence).
quote: The LLM crowd outperforms a simple no-information benchmark and is not statistically different from the human crowd.
limits: Only 31 questions; the equivalence bounds are wide (0.081 Brier). The crowd was twelve different model families, not samples of one model. Best single model (0.15) beat the crowd median, so crowd gain over best member was not shown.
agent_relevance: Crowd of different models can match a human crowd, but it did not beat its best member. Aggregating weak with strong can cost accuracy.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) Study 2: exposing LLMs to human median forecasts
finding: Giving GPT-4 and Claude 2 the human median forecast improved their accuracy, but plain averaging of human and machine forecasts was better still.
numbers: Accuracy gain 17% to 28%. Example Brier 0.22 (SD 0.19) to 0.15 (SD 0.14), p<0.001.
limits: Two models; 31 questions; the shown value was a crowd median, so the model could copy it.
agent_relevance: Showing a model a crowd answer moves it toward that answer, a conformity effect. Averaging in code beats asking the model to integrate (G5).

source: Li, Zhang, Yu, Fu, Ye (2024) More Agents Is All You Need, TMLR
finding: Sampling the same model many times and taking a majority vote raises accuracy as the ensemble grows; gains are largest on mid-hard tasks and shrink at extreme difficulty.
numbers: GSM8K: Llama2-13B at 15 samples matches Llama2-70B single; Llama2-70B at 15 and GPT-3.5-Turbo at 20 match their larger counterparts. Gains peak at inherent difficulty 100-200 then taper at 400 in their difficulty scan. Averages over 10 runs.
limits: Tasks with a clear answer string to vote on. Accuracy still rises with size, which shows the errors are partly random, but no test of how fast it saturates.
agent_relevance: Same-model voting works when single-sample errors are partly random. It cannot fix errors every sample shares (see b19). Supports voting as a hint (G4), not proof.

source: Smit, Grinsztajn, Duckworth, Barrett, Pretorius (2024) Should we be going MAD?, ICML
finding: Multi-agent debate protocols did not reliably beat self-consistency or single-agent baselines; some became better after hyperparameter tuning, so they are more sensitive and hard to tune.
numbers: Best-system table, first dataset: Self-Consistency 0.60, Single Agent 0.60, Medprompt 0.65, Society of Mind 0.64, Multi-Persona 0.58. Another dataset: Self-Consistency 0.78 vs Single Agent 0.76 vs Multi-Persona 0.72.
limits: Accuracy differences of 0.01-0.05 on mid-size benchmarks; dataset names were not verified in my extraction of the layout-mangled table.
agent_relevance: Communication between agents has not been shown to beat independent samples plus a vote. Keep samples independent (G4).

source: Wang, Wang, Su, Tong, Song (2024) Rethinking the Bounds of LLM Reasoning: Are Multi-Agent Discussions the Key?
finding: A single agent with a strong prompt (with demonstrations) matches the best multi-agent discussion; discussion helps mainly when the prompt has no demonstrations. Discussion sometimes turns a correct single-agent answer into a wrong consensus.
numbers: Quantitative table not extracted; paper reports multi-agent beats single only without demonstrations. MAD (disagree-on-purpose) was the weakest framework on ChatGPT-3.5.
limits: ChatGPT-3.5 mostly; reasoning tasks including FOLIO-wiki.
agent_relevance: Forcing disagreement (persona dissent) hurt; conforms to G4 (no persona voters) and G1 (no forced doubt).

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Stop Overvaluing Multi-Agent Debate
finding: Across 5 debate methods, 9 benchmarks and 4 models, debate often failed to beat chain-of-thought or self-consistency, but mixing two different models (heterogeneity) consistently helped.
numbers: Heter-SoM +6.4% over the average of its two single-model SoM runs; Heter-EoT +8.2% over EoT-average; all heterogeneous MAD up to +5.8% over CoT-average.
limits: Gain is measured against the average of the two models, not the better one. Two candidate models (GPT and Llama).
agent_relevance: Diversity helps when the models differ in what they get wrong, which is the Condorcet independence condition. Compare against the best member before crediting diversity.

source: Li, Lin, Xia, Jin (2025) Rethinking Mixture-of-Agents: Is Mixing Different LLMs Beneficial? (Self-MoA)
finding: Aggregating many samples from the single best model beat mixing several different models in most settings, because mixing lowers average quality. Quality mattered more than diversity.
numbers: Self-MoA +6.6 points over Mixed-MoA on AlpacaEval 2.0; average +3.8% across MMLU, CRUX, MATH. In a task-mixture built to favour mixing, only two of 13 mixes beat Self-MoA, by 0.17% and 0.35%. Over 200 experiments; Vendi score for diversity.
limits: Aggregation is a model-written synthesis, not a vote. Models in the pool differed widely in quality. Their reproduction of the original MoA single-proposer result differed from the original.
agent_relevance: Direct rival to b17: diversity helps only if members are about equally good. Rule: add a different voter only if its measured accuracy is near the best.

source: Kim, Garg, Peng, Garg (2025) Correlated Errors in Large Language Models, ICML
finding: Different LLMs make the same wrong answers far more often than chance; bigger, more accurate models are more correlated; same developer, architecture and size raise correlation.
numbers: Over 350 LLMs, two leaderboards (HuggingFace, HELM) plus a resume task. Models agree 60% of the time when both are wrong (abstract). Mean pair agreement on errors 0.423 on HuggingFace. Some pairs 0.97 (two Llama variants). Regression features explain 34-62% of error agreement.
limits: Multiple-choice agreement rate; resume ratings use human ratings as imperfect truth.
agent_relevance: This is the main modern failure of the independence condition. Errors are shared across vendors, so voting across models does not remove them (G4). Capability growth makes it worse.

source: Kim et al. (2025) Correlated Errors: downstream LLM-as-judge
finding: A judge model inflates the score of models that are less accurate than itself because they share wrong answers, and under-credits models better than itself.
numbers: Pattern reported across judges; exact inflation sizes not extracted.
limits: Judge test on leaderboard items.
agent_relevance: A model judge is a voter with correlated errors. Supports G5 (code selects, judge blind to authorship).

source: Goel et al. (2025) Great Models Think Alike and this Undermines AI Oversight, ICML
finding: With a chance-adjusted similarity measure (CAPA), LLM judges favour models whose mistakes resemble their own, after controlling for accuracy; mistakes are becoming more similar as models improve.
numbers: Average Pearson r=0.84 between judge score and similarity; example: Qwen2.5-72B judge scores Qwen2.5-7B at 71% correct and the more capable Llama-3.1-70B at 67% (MCQ accuracy 41% vs 51%). Weak-to-strong gain correlates with similarity at r=-0.35 (p<0.01) after controlling for accuracy gap.
limits: MMLU-Pro and similar; CAPA is a new metric.
agent_relevance: Gives a measurable independence number. Use chance-adjusted agreement, not raw agreement, to decide if an extra voter adds information.

source: Wenger and Kenett (2025) We're Different, We're the Same: Creative Homogeneity Across LLMs
finding: Across 22 LLMs, creative answers were far more similar to each other than answers of different humans were to each other, even after controlling for response structure.
numbers: 22 LLMs vs Prolific humans (N=102) on Alternative Uses, Forward Flow and Divergent Association tests; variability tested with t-tests (e.g. AUT t(1046)=11.0, p<0.001 in one comparison with a prior human study).
limits: Creativity tests, not correctness. Human sample is small and online. Same model family more homogeneous.
agent_relevance: A crowd of models is a crowd with low diversity. Diversity must be created by tools, data or problem reformulation, not by changing the model name.

source: Kaesberg, Becker, Wahle, Ruas, Gipp (2025) Voting or Consensus? Decision-Making in Multi-Agent Debate
finding: Changing only the decision rule in multi-agent debate, voting beat consensus on reasoning tasks and consensus beat voting on knowledge tasks. More agents helped; more discussion rounds before voting hurt.
numbers: Voting +13.2% on reasoning tasks; consensus +2.8% on knowledge tasks; on reasoning tasks vote beat consensus by 13.1% on SQuAD 2.0, 0.2% on StrategyQA, 26.4% on MuSR. All-Agents Drafting +3.3%, Collective Improvement +7.4% over baseline (adds answer diversity).
limits: Few models; relative gains in percent.
agent_relevance: More discussion before voting reduces accuracy, which matches the conformity story: talking removes independence. Vote first, then discuss only on disagreement (G1).

source: Du et al. (2023) Improving factuality and reasoning via multiagent debate (as cited in b15, b16, b17)
finding: Original debate claims that rounds of debate improve factuality are the thing b15-b17 fail to reproduce against equal-compute baselines.
numbers: Not read directly.
limits: Cited via other papers only.
agent_relevance: Debate gains often disappear when the baseline gets the same compute.

source: Condorcet (1785) Essai; Ladha (1992) correlated-votes version; Surowiecki (2004)
finding: Majority accuracy tends to 1 as voters grow only if each is right more than half the time and votes are independent; with correlated votes the gain stops at a ceiling set by the correlation.
numbers: Not re-read. Standard result; Ladha 1992 (Am J Pol Sci) cited from memory.
limits: Not fetched this session. Also fails if voters are right less than half the time: the majority tends to the wrong answer.
agent_relevance: b19 says LLM errors correlate (pair agreement on errors about 0.4-0.6), so the ceiling is far below 1 and a systematically wrong answer gets wronger with more votes.

source: Vul and Pashler (2008) Measuring the crowd within, Psychological Science 19(7)
finding: Averaging a person's two guesses beat one guess; gain was larger when the second guess came 3 weeks later.
numbers: Per a search summary: gain intervals about 2.5-10.4% immediate and 11.6-20.4% delayed; t(172)=3.94 delayed. Not verified from the paper.
limits: Original download failed; replication numbers in b01 are read, these are not.
agent_relevance: Time and context change create independence; same-prompt resamples are the weakest case.
